report:
# Research Findings: Do Wax Coatings on Apples Cause Cancer?

**Short answer: No — there is no credible scientific evidence for this claim.**

**What the wax actually is:** Food-grade waxes used on apples (carnauba wax, shellac, and sometimes petroleum-based waxes) replace the fruit's natural wax removed during washing. They are applied to reduce moisture loss and extend shelf life (https://www.star-k.org/articles/articles/1128/facts-on-wax-are-vegetables-and-fruit-waxes-kosher/).

**Regulatory safety assessments:** Carnauba wax (E903) and shellac (E904) have been formally re-evaluated by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), which concluded their currently authorized food uses "would not be of safety concern." The FDA similarly designates these waxes as safe for food-contact use (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0308814619306181). Notably, EFSA's 2024 re-evaluation flagged a separate, narrow concern — trace organochlorine impurities in *wax-free* shellac from certain bleaching processes — but this is unrelated to wax itself and doesn't apply to the wax-containing shellac used on apples.

**Fact-checking consensus:** Snopes directly investigated the "wax on apples causes cancer" claim and found it false, noting the wax itself is indigestible and passes through the body without being absorbed, and citing no known carcinogens among common fruit waxes (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/wax-on-apples-causes-cancer/).

**The real, legitimate concern:** The actual food-safety issue isn't the wax—it's that wax coatings can potentially trap pesticide residues underneath, making them harder to wash off, as some more recent studies on washing effectiveness note (https://nypost.com/2024/08/12/health/youre-eating-apples-wrong-washing-fruit-does-not-remove-pesticides-study-finds/). This is a pesticide-residue issue, not evidence that wax itself is carcinogenic.

**Conclusion:** The claim that food-grade wax on apples causes cancer is unsupported by regulatory reviews or fact-checking investigations. If concerned, focus on washing/peeling to reduce pesticide residue rather than avoiding wax itself.
